text: Poor diet directly causes some diseases — for example piglets not getting enough iron develop anemia — and in general, any nutrient deficiency reduces disease resistance and impairs growth and reproduction. Water: needed for blood circulation, digestion, milk production, and urination; insufficient water reduces appetite and increases risk of cystitis, and poor water quality (bacterial contamination, pesticides, or virus shedding such as ducks shedding Bird Flu into a pond) can itself transmit disease. Energy: mainly supplied by starches (e.g. cassava root) and fats (e.g. rice bran); a deficiency forces the animal to draw on fat reserves and lose weight — for example a lactating sow needing a lot of energy to milk piglets will end weaning very thin, with health problems and a delayed return to oestrus, if she cannot eat enough; too much energy causes obesity, difficulty standing, and difficult farrowing. Protein: the basis of body structure, made of amino acids; pigs and poultry need certain essential amino acids (e.g. lysine, methionine) supplied in feed (fishmeal >50% protein, soybean 40%, rice bran 12%, corn 8%, rice 2%), while cattle can synthesize all their amino acids from fiber; protein deficiency causes poor growth (muscle cannot develop), low milk production, and weak piglets or calves. Minerals: calcium, phosphorus, and manganese support bone, teeth, and tissue growth; other minerals are needed in small amounts but are essential (e.g. injecting iron into newborn piglets to prevent anemia); calcium deficiency causes rickets in young animals or thin-shelled eggs in layers, and phosphorus deficiency causes muscular weakness and poor fertility. Vitamins: essential for metabolism and nutrient use, needed only in small amounts but crucial; bright, smooth hair and supple skin are good indicators of adequate vitamin supply, while a poor coat can suggest deficiency.
